paper.summary: Moment measures of skewness and kurtosis are driven by the tails: one extreme value can dominate them. We propose shape coefficients built on the half central moment, the expected square root of the deviation from the mean. Negative deviations have imaginary roots, so its real part collects the deviations above the mean and its imaginary part those below. The Asymmetry coefficient, from the angle of this moment, lies strictly between $-1$ and $1$; it is determined by the probability on each side of the mean and by how evenly the deviations spread on each side, and it places the mean as an $L_{1.5}$-quantile. Hypotailedness, the absolute half moment scaled by the square root of the standard deviation, and the Extremity coefficient derived from it measure, as kurtosis does, how far the squared standardised deviations spread from one, but give values near the mean more weight and values in the tails less. We derive the influence functions, showing that they grow linearly for Asymmetry and quadratically for Hypotailedness. We also derive the sharp lower bound of the sample Hypotailedness, the asymptotic normality of the sample coefficients, and closed forms for seven standard distributions. In simulations we show that the sample Asymmetry is nearly unbiased, while Hypotailedness is biased upwards in small samples. Finally, on rock samples and four stock index return series, the coefficients change far less than moment skewness and kurtosis when the most extreme values are removed, and Extremity separates the rock variables best among tail-weight measures.

definitions.definition: The half central moment (HCM) of a variable $y$ with finite mean $\mu_1$: $$\mu_{0.5} = \mathrm{E}\left[(y - \mu_1)^{0.5}\right]$$, the square root taken as the principal root, so that $$\mu_{0.5} = \mathrm{E}\left[(y-\mu_1)_+^{0.5}\right] + i\,\mathrm{E}\left[(\mu_1-y)_+^{0.5}\right]$$: the real part $\mathcal{R}$ comes from the values above the mean and the imaginary part $\mathcal{I}$ from those below it. Sample estimate: $$m_{0.5} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} (y_j - m_1)^{0.5}$$, with $m_1$ the sample mean.

The half absolute moment (HAM): $$\nu_{0.5} = \mathcal{R}(\mu_{0.5}) + \mathcal{I}(\mu_{0.5}) = \mathrm{E}|y - \mu_1|^{0.5}$$; sample estimate $$v_{0.5} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} |y_j - m_1|^{0.5}$$.

$$\mathrm{Asymmetry} = 1 - \frac{4\phi}{\pi} = \frac{4}{\pi}\arctan\left(\frac{\mathcal{R}(\mu_{0.5}) - \mathcal{I}(\mu_{0.5})}{\nu_{0.5}}\right),$$ where $\phi = \mathrm{Arg}(\mu_{0.5}) \in \left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$; positive when the part above the mean is the larger. The sample coefficient uses $m_{0.5}$ and $v_{0.5}$.

$\mathrm{Hypotailedness} = \frac{\nu_{0.5}}{\sigma^{0.5}}$ for a variable with finite positive variance $\sigma^2$; the sample coefficient divides $v_{0.5}$ by $\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j}(y_j - m_1)^2\right)^{0.25}$.
$\mathrm{Extremity} = 2\,\mathrm{Hypotailedness}^{p} - 1$ with $p = \frac{\log 0.5}{\log(2 \times 3^{-0.75})} \approx 5.30$, so that the uniform distribution has Extremity 0.
$\mathrm{CH} = \frac{\mu_{0.5}}{\sigma^{0.5}}$, the half central moment divided by the square root of the standard deviation (the manuscript of 19 November 2026).

For a variable with finite variance and deviation $D = y - \mu_1$: $$H_+ = \frac{\mathrm{E}\left[D^{0.5} \mid D > 0\right]}{\left(\mathrm{E}\left[D^2 \mid D > 0\right]\right)^{0.25}}$$ above the mean and $$H_- = \frac{\mathrm{E}\left[|D|^{0.5} \mid D < 0\right]}{\left(\mathrm{E}\left[D^2 \mid D < 0\right]\right)^{0.25}}$$ below it; in a sample, the same ratios over the values above and below the sample mean.

The bounded Complex Extremity proposed in this study: $\mathrm{CE} = \left(2H_+^{p} - 1\right) + i\left(2H_-^{p} - 1\right)$, with $H_\pm$ the one-sided Hypotailedness and $p = \frac{\log 0.5}{\log(2 \times 3^{-0.75})}$; the real part describes the values above the mean.
The standardised third central moment $\frac{\mathrm{E}[(y-\mu_1)^3]}{\sigma^3}$; sample version with $\frac{1}{n}$ moments.
The standardised fourth central moment minus 3, $\frac{\mathrm{E}[(y-\mu_1)^4]}{\sigma^4} - 3$; sample version with $\frac{1}{n}$ moments.
The L-moment ratio $\tau_3 = \frac{\lambda_3}{\lambda_2}$; sample version from unbiased probability-weighted moments.
The L-moment ratio $\tau_4 = \frac{\lambda_4}{\lambda_2}$; sample version from unbiased probability-weighted moments.
The trimmed L-moment ratio $\tau_3^{(1)}$ with trimming (1,1), which exists without moments.
The trimmed L-moment ratio $\tau_4^{(1)}$ with trimming (1,1).

Bowley's quartile skewness $\frac{Q_3 + Q_1 - 2Q_2}{Q_3 - Q_1}$, the member at $u = \frac{1}{4}$ of the quantile skewness family of Groeneveld & Meeden (1984); sample quartiles by linear interpolation (R type 7).
The medcouple, a robust skewness measure in $[-1, 1]$ built from the median of a kernel over pairs of values on either side of the median.

Skewness centred at the mean, $2F(\mu_1) - 1$ ($F$ the distribution function), bounded in $[-1, 1]$ and positive for right-skewed distributions, the same sign convention as moment skewness; the bounded form used by Eberl & Klar (2020) of Tajuddin's (1996) log-odds $\log\frac{F(\mu_1)}{1 - F(\mu_1)}$. Sample version $2\hat F(m_1) - 1$, the share of values at or below the sample mean, rescaled.
Moors octile kurtosis $\frac{(E_7 - E_5) + (E_3 - E_1)}{E_6 - E_2}$, $E_k$ the $k$-th octile; sample octiles by R type 7.
The ratio of the mean absolute deviation to the standard deviation, $\frac{\mathrm{E}|y-\mu_1|}{\sigma}$, the order-one analogue of Hypotailedness.

The coefficients built on the half central moment that the study compares with other measures: [[D3:Asymmetry coefficient]], [[D4:Hypotailedness]], [[D5:Extremity coefficient]] and [[D8:Complex Extremity]].

The measures the half-moment coefficients are compared with: for skewness, [[D9:moment skewness]], [[D11:L-skewness]], [[D13:TL-skewness]], [[D15:quartile skewness]], [[D16:medcouple]] and [[D17:mean-based skewness]]; for tail weight, [[D10:excess kurtosis]], [[D12:L-kurtosis]], [[D14:TL-kurtosis]], [[D18:octile kurtosis]] and [[D19:Geary ratio]].

Samples of size $n$ drawn from a base distribution with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$; in each, the first value is replaced by $\mu + k\sigma$. Every measure is computed on the clean sample and on the contaminated one.

For one measure, base distribution, $n$ and $k$: the mean over replications of the measure on the contaminated samples minus its mean on the clean samples, divided by the standard deviation of the measure over the clean samples.
Measurements on 48 rock samples from a petroleum reservoir (BP research), the rock data set of R's datasets package: area, perimeter, shape and permeability.

Daily closing prices of four European stock indices (DAX, SMI, CAC, FTSE), 1991-1998, business days, 1860 observations each: the EuStockMarkets data set of R's datasets package; analysed as daily log returns (1859 each).
Every measure computed on the first $t$ returns of a series, for every $t$ from 30 to the full length.

claims.statement: For a variable with a finite positive variance $\sigma^2$, let $V = \frac{(y - \mu_1)^2}{\sigma^2}$, the squared standardised deviation, whose mean is 1, and $g(v) = \frac{3 + v}{4} - v^{0.25}$. Then one minus the [[D4:Hypotailedness]] equals $\mathrm{E}[g(V)]$, the [[D5:Extremity coefficient]] equals $2(1 - \mathrm{E}[g(V)])^p - 1$ and so decreases as $\mathrm{E}[g(V)]$ grows, and, with a finite fourth moment, the [[D10:excess kurtosis]] plus 2 equals $\mathrm{E}[(V - 1)^2]$. The function $g$ is strictly convex and zero only at $v = 1$, is $\frac{3}{32}(v - 1)^2 + O(|v - 1|^3)$ near 1, is $\frac{3}{4}$ at $v = 0$, and is $\frac{v}{4} + O(v^{0.25})$ for large $v$. So Hypotailedness, Extremity and kurtosis all measure how far $V$ spreads from 1: Hypotailedness through the loss $g$, kurtosis through the loss $(v - 1)^2$. Scaled by $\frac{32}{3}$, so that it agrees with $(v - 1)^2$ to second order at $v = 1$, the loss $g$ gives a value at the mean 8 times the weight the kurtosis loss gives it, and a value far out a weight linear rather than quadratic in $V$.

(6) Taylor at 1: g''(1)/2 = 3/32; g'''(v) = -(21/64) v^(-11/4) is bounded near 1, so the remainder is O(|v-1|^3); the cubic coefficient is -7/128. Holds. (7) g(0) = 3/4 = 24/32 = 8 * (3/32)(0-1)^2. Holds. (8) g(v) - v/4 = 3/4 - v^(1/4) = O(v^(1/4)) as v -> inf. Holds. Analysis: For each measure, base distribution, n and k: the standardised shift (mean over replications of the measure on contaminated samples minus its mean on clean samples, divided by its standard deviation on clean samples) with its Monte Carlo standard error; and for each measure, base distribution and n, the growth exponent: the slope of log |standardised shift| on log k over k = 10, 20, 50, 100, to set beside the influence functions of H17 (Q1).

evidence.description: Lab runs RN20 under plan PL12. Design: Sensitivity to the few most extreme values. On each of the eight data sets (Area, Perimeter, Shape, Permeability: 48 values each; the daily log returns of DAX, SMI, CAC, FTSE: 1859 each), every measure is computed on all values and again without the k values farthest from the mean (largest absolute deviation), k = 1, 2 and 3; the change is divided by the measure's bootstrap standard error on all values, so that it reads in units of its own sampling noise. Run: benefits.py sensitivity. evidence.description: Lab runs RN21 under plan PL13. Design: Precision. On each of the eight data sets, the bootstrap standard error of every measure; then, for each measure and each group of four data sets (the rock variables; the index return series), the discrimination ratio: the standard deviation of the measure over the four data sets divided by the root mean square of their bootstrap standard errors. Run: benefits.py precision. Analysis: The bootstrap standard errors by measure and data set, and the discrimination ratios by measure and group, reported in full; a measure with a higher ratio tells the data sets of a group apart further beyond its own noise.

evidence.description: Lab runs RN22 under plan PL14. Design: Stability over time. On the daily log returns of each index, every measure is computed on each window of 260 consecutive returns (about a trading year), moving one return at a time (1600 windows). For each measure and index: the spike ratio, the largest change between consecutive windows divided by the measure's standard deviation over all windows, and the roughness, the median change divided by the same standard deviation. Run: benefits.py stability. Analysis: The spike ratios and roughness by measure and index, reported in full; a high spike ratio means one day can move the measure by a large share of its whole range over the period.

limitations.statement: Run RN6 departed from plan PL1 in the numerical check of the influence functions only: the central difference $\frac{T(F_\varepsilon) - T(F_{-\varepsilon})}{2\varepsilon}$ with $\varepsilon = \frac{10^{-6}}{1 + k^2}$ replaced the one-sided difference with $\varepsilon = 10^{-6}$, and the error of an influence-function value was measured against $\max(|\text{value}|, 1)$, because the one-sided difference is too coarse for the tolerance $10^{-8}$ and the influence functions cross zero; the proofs and the other checks followed the plan.
The robustness and sampling studies use three base distributions (normal, Student t(5), exponential) and one kind of contamination, a single value moved along the line mean + k standard deviations.
The real-data results describe two data sets, 48 rock samples and the 1991-1998 returns of four indices; whether the coefficients are easier to interpret than skewness and kurtosis is not tested.
The comparison of robustness and precision uses two groups of four data sets and summarises each group by medians; the discrimination ratio depends on which data sets are grouped together.

The first value of a sample of n = 1000 is replaced by the mean plus k standard deviations; each line is a measure's standardised shift (absolute value) against k, for normal, Student t (5 degrees of freedom) and exponential samples, on logarithmic axes. The slope of a line at large k is the measure's growth exponent: excess kurtosis and moment skewness climb fastest, Hypotailedness next, Asymmetry and Extremity at about the rate of L-skewness and L-kurtosis, and the medcouple stays flat.

Asymmetry is nearly unbiased and covers close to 95%; Extremity and Hypotailedness are biased upwards in small samples and their intervals under-cover for the heavier-tailed and skewed distributions.
